role: Analog IC Design Engineer (junior, power management chips)
headline: In the second year after a master's in microelectronics, drawing LDOs and bandgap references at a power-management chip company in Xiamen, running Monte Carlo in Virtuoso all night over a fraction of a millivolt of temperature drift, and waiting for the first chip of your own to come back from the fab: an analog IC design engineer
unit: The analog design department of a fabless power-management chip company in the Torch High-Tech Zone, Xiamen
education: Master's degree in microelectronics and solid-state electronics
level: You're fluent in Virtuoso and Spectre, can explain how op-amps, bandgaps and LDOs work, and run your own process corners and Monte Carlo. But your mentor still has to help you with loop stability, extracting the layout's parasitics turns your simulation results upside down, and you've never yet seen a chip of yours actually running on a test board.
intro: Your master's was a low-noise bandgap reference, and you signed with this power-management chip company in Xiamen to draw analog circuits under a mentor with fifteen years in. Your chips go into phones, power banks, power tools and cars, turning battery power into the small, steady voltage a chip needs. From today on, whether that small slice of voltage holds steady in millions of chips depends partly on the few dozen transistors you draw.
salary_note: Estimate: the pay-by-experience figures for analog design lean toward the big firms of Shanghai and Shenzhen; analog chip companies in Xiamen pay a little over ten percent less, but housing prices and the pace are both gentler. In down years for the industry the bonus shrinks by half, and the options wait on an IPO.

facts.label: Junior Analog IC Design Engineer (current level)
facts.value: 0-2 years, ¥18,700–27,500 a month (national average, derived from pay by experience)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Bench work in the test lab: boards, curves, failure causes

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Writing design documents, test reports and datasheets

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 65 related listings nationwide, 1 in this city (mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: From your rented room in Jimei you take the BRT onto the island, the sea gray and hazy under the bridge. Downstairs at the software park you eat a bowl of satay noodles with an extra portion of intestines.

You open the Monte Carlo run left on the server last night: five hundred runs, seven with the bandgap output voltage out of spec. You pull out the device parameters for those seven and go through them to see which transistor pair wasn't matched.

Your mentor comes to look at your LDO loop, draws a line on your screen and says the phase margin is only thirty-five degrees; one load step and it'll oscillate. You change the compensation capacitor and run it again.

Lunch with the layout engineer. She says the input pair you gave her is placed too far apart to match well. You say you thought further apart would dissipate heat better. She laughs and says she'll come show you in the afternoon.

In the afternoon, at her screen, she points it out cell by cell: common-centroid placement, dummy devices, guard rings. You fill a page with notes, then go back and resize the circuit's devices again.

Extracting parasitics for post-layout simulation, the results come out well below pre-layout: power-supply rejection down eight decibels. You go through the layout trace by trace and find a ground line routed too long.

Before leaving, your mentor brings a sample of the previous generation's chip, solders it onto a test board, hooks up an electronic load and an oscilloscope, and has you watch how much the output voltage wobbles when the load jumps from zero to one amp. You stare at that curve for a long time.
Back in your rented room you draw the loop's Bode plot in your notebook, three times, and only the third matches the simulation. The sea breeze comes in through the window with a taste of salt.

ladder.title: Junior Analog IC Design Engineer
ladder.focus: Draw blocks, run process corners and Monte Carlo, and do post-layout simulation with the layout team under a mentor. You move up by taking a block through tape-out on your own and having it pass on silicon.

ladder.title: Analog IC Design Engineer
ladder.focus: Own several blocks in a chip on your own, from breaking down the spec to testing returned silicon.

ladder.title: Senior Analog IC Design Engineer
ladder.focus: Own a chip's entire analog section on your own, mentor newcomers, and discuss specs with customers.

ladder.title: Staff Analog IC Design Engineer / Design Manager
ladder.focus: Lead a team, own a product line's circuit architecture and spec definition, and sign off tape-outs.

ladder.title: Director of Analog Design / Chief Engineer
ladder.focus: Run the analog design teams, answerable for the technical roadmap, process choices and tape-out risk.

ai_tasks.name: Writing design documents, test reports and datasheets
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft design documents, test reports and datasheets from simulation data, test data and templates, and plot the curves automatically. A person only needs to spot-check the key parameters, test conditions and conclusions.

ai_tasks.name: Tuning circuit parameters, running process corners and Monte Carlo
ai_tasks.how: AI-assisted optimization tools can sweep thousands of device sizings overnight and run corners and Monte Carlo in bulk, organizing the results. Transistor-level trade-offs, compromises between specs and the final sign-off rest on an engineer's judgment.

ai_tasks.name: Checking layout DRC/LVS and reading parasitics
ai_tasks.how: AI can help check DRC/LVS errors, sort the differences before and after parasitic extraction and flag risks. Layout trade-offs such as matching, routing and shielding, and the back-and-forth with the layout engineer, are still for a person to settle.

ai_tasks.name: Answering customers' technical questions and building reference designs
ai_tasks.how: AI can search the literature, draft replies, and generate reference designs and evaluation-board notes. How to read a problem at the customer's site, how to reproduce it, and whether a reference design really works, a person has to verify.

ai_tasks.name: Bench work in the test lab: boards, curves, failure causes
ai_tasks.how: Soldering boards, hooking up oscilloscopes and network analyzers, keeping watch at the thermal chamber, decapping chips under the microscope: finding the root cause of a failure takes a person's hands and experience. AI can only help process data and draw plots.

ai_tasks.name: Setting specs, judging tape-out risk, answering for mass production
ai_tasks.how: How to trade off the spec, whether this chip can go to tape-out, and who carries it if mass production goes wrong involve cross-team coordination and millions of yuan in mask costs. The direction and the responsibility rest with people.

events.e_first_si: The first LDO you drew came back from the fab. In the test lab you soldered it onto a board, hands a little unsteady, and powered it up: a flat line on the oscilloscope. Your mentor, beside you, said: not bad. You stood in the test lab a long while before leaving.
events.e_oscillate: One chip came back and oscillated at light load, with the datasheet already printed. You and your mentor lived in the test lab for two weeks, and finally found a package inductance the simulation hadn't accounted for. A respin meant another three months; at the retrospective you spoke alone for half an hour.
events.e_mass: The charging chip you owned went into mass production, millions of units in the first batch. In a mall you saw a power-bank brand, looked it up when you got back, and found it used your company's chip.
events.e_customer: A batch of a customer's product came back: the chip would occasionally reset at high temperature. You went with the applications engineer to the customer's factory and kept watch at the thermal chamber for three days, and found the customer's board used the wrong capacitor. You wrote a report, and the customer's engineers took you out for tea.
events.e_ai_sizing: The company bought an AI-assisted circuit optimization tool. You give it the specs and constraints, and overnight it sweeps thousands of device sizings and picks the best few. Reading the results the next morning, you found it had pushed a transistor pair's length to the process limit for a little extra gain, and you added that to the constraints.
events.e_ai_doc: AI can now draft datasheets and test reports from simulation and test data, and plot the curves automatically. A datasheet that used to cost you two late nights gets handed in within a day. Spot-checking, you found it had a temperature condition the wrong way round, and you added a check to the template.
events.e_ai_layout: The layout side got automatic placement tools too, and digital and simple analog cells can be placed automatically now. But the most critical input pair, the layout engineer still drew herself, cell by cell. She said the machine doesn't yet understand what "symmetrical in just the right way" means.
events.e_cycle: The consumer electronics market went cold, downstream inventory piled up, and chip prices fell thirty percent in one quarter. The company paused two new projects, the bonus shrank by half, and two people left your team. You stayed, and had more work in your hands than before.
events.e_domestic: The wave of switching to Chinese-made chips arrived, and several big customers making appliances and power tools came to you for replacements. That year you revised five chips on your own, and the test-lab lights burned until midnight every day.
events.e_capacity: Fab capacity was tight, and one of your tape-outs got pushed back two months. You used the time to rerun that chip's Monte Carlo and found a risk hiding in a corner case, which you fixed before your slot came up.
events.e_ipo: The company listed on the STAR Market, and on the day of the bell-ringing everyone watched the livestream on the big screen. After your options vested you sold some, and moved to a smaller flat on the island, closer to the sea.
events.e_poach: In one week you took four headhunter calls, all looking for analog engineers with tape-out experience. You told your manager, who said there'd be a raise next month. You didn't leave.
events.e_typhoon: A typhoon came and the whole city shut down, work and school. The internet went down at home, so you got out pen and paper and derived an op-amp's transfer function. It took the afternoon, and outside, a tree came down.
events.e_house: You bought a flat in Haicang. The down payment emptied your savings, and you borrowed some from family too. On handover day you stood on the balcony and could see, across the water, the island and its buildings.
events.e_wedding: You got married. The wedding photos were taken on Gulangyu, and the photographer had you stand under a great banyan for an hour. You were dripping with sweat, still thinking about that chip's temperature drift.
events.e_child: Your child was born. For those months you rocked the baby to sleep at home with your phone in your hand, watching the curves the test lab sent. The baby fell asleep, and the curves flattened out.
events.e_checkup: The health check said straightened cervical spine and high uric acid. The doctor told you to eat less seafood. You thought of Xiamen's satay noodles and oyster omelets, and sighed.
events.e_parents: Your mother went into hospital back home in Jiangxi, and you took a week off to go. In the ward the heart monitor beeped, and watching its line, you found yourself wondering where its noise came from.
events.e_master_leave: The mentor who trained you was poached by a big company in Shanghai. On the day he left, he copied you a folder of test curves from every failed chip of his fifteen years, every file named "Never Again."
events.e_apprentice: The first chip of the newcomer you mentor came back and passed on the first try. He ran over with the test board to show you. You glanced at the oscilloscope and said: not bad. Then you were the first to laugh.
events.e_eyes: Years of staring at waveforms and layouts tire your eyes more and more easily. You started walking a stretch of the Island Ring Road every evening, watching ships move slowly across the sea, measuring nothing.

c_aitool.title: Let AI tune your circuits, or tune by hand first?
c_aitool.situation: The department is trialing an AI-assisted analog circuit optimization tool, and your manager asks who'll learn it first and work out how everyone should use it. But your mentor says the young ones shouldn't touch it yet: only after tuning a few hundred circuits by hand do you know where the machine's results are wrong.

options.label: Learn the AI tool first
options.result: In half a year you worked out how to give it specs and constraints, and wrote it up as the department's guide. Tuning an op-amp went from a week to two days.

options.label: Tune by hand first
options.result: You listened to your mentor and that year tuned dozens of circuits by hand, drawing a Bode plot for each in your notebook. Later, looking at what the AI produced, you could tell at a glance which set was lying.

c_lab.title: Live in the test lab, or leave it to the test engineers?
c_lab.situation: Your chip is back, and the test engineer says he'll handle the testing so you can draw the next one. But you want to go to the test lab yourself, starting from soldering boards and hooking up instruments, and see curve by curve what your own work really looks like.

options.label: Live in the test lab
options.result: You spent a month in the test lab, learned the probe station and the network analyzer, and wrote down curve by curve where the measurements differed from simulation.

options.label: Hand it to test and keep drawing
options.result: You handed off the testing and turned in the second chip's layout a month early. When the test engineer's report came, you understood half of it and went to ask him about the rest.

c_senior.title: Promotion review: Senior Analog IC Design Engineer
c_senior.situation: Your manager says you can apply for Senior Analog IC Design Engineer this year: owning a chip's whole analog section on your own, from spec definition and circuit design through layout to silicon testing, and mentoring a newcomer. At the review you'll present the chips you've taped out, and why one of them failed.

options.label: Go for the review
options.result: You talked about the chip that oscillated at light load, and the package inductance the simulation missed. A veteran expert on the panel asked how you account for packaging in simulation now. You pulled up your model and answered.

options.label: Give it another year
options.result: You said you wanted to tape out one more chip. That year you did a DC-DC converter that passed on its first silicon, and the next year's review file was twice as thick.

c_shanghai.title: A big Shanghai company makes a big offer
c_shanghai.situation: A big power-chip company in Zhangjiang, Shanghai, wants you, for thirty percent more and bigger projects, including automotive and server chips. But you'd be leaving Xiamen, the flat you just got the keys to and the evenings by the sea, and housing in Shanghai costs twice as much.

options.label: Go to Shanghai
options.result: In Shanghai you did server power chips, a single chip carrying hundreds of amps, and for the first time you knew what heat really meant. Taking the high-speed train back to Xiamen at weekends, you could smell the sea the moment you left the station.

options.label: Stay in Xiamen
options.result: You turned it down. That weekend you cycled the Island Ring Road from Zengcuo'an to Yefengzhai, then came home and went over the next chip's spec once more.

c_auto.title: Move to automotive-grade chips
c_auto.situation: The company is entering the auto market and setting up an automotive chip team, to build from scratch a power chip that passes automotive reliability qualification: forty below to a hundred and fifty degrees, and no failures for over a decade. The project cycle is three times a consumer chip's, but if it works, you'll be among the first at the company who understand automotive.

options.label: Go automotive
options.result: Two and a half years on the automotive project, and the chip passed every reliability qualification. When the carmaker's engineers came to audit the factory, their first question was about failure analysis. You answered for half an hour.

options.label: Stay in consumer
options.result: You stayed in consumer, three tape-outs a year, fast pace, high volume. You became the person in the department with the most chips taped out.

c_expert.title: Apply for Staff Analog IC Design Engineer / Design Manager
c_expert.situation: The department is creating a Staff Analog IC Design Engineer / Design Manager post: leading seven or eight people, owning a product line's circuit architecture and spec definition, with the final signature on whether each chip goes to tape-out. If you get it, most of your circuit-drawing time goes, replaced by reviews, staffing, and negotiating specs with marketing and customers.

options.label: Apply
options.result: Your pitch was one table: how each of the department's failed chips had failed over the years, and which processes changed afterwards. The director asked which risks were still open. You went through them one by one.

options.label: Stay hands-on
options.result: You recommended a colleague and kept chewing on the hardest chip, the low-noise reference. Whenever young engineers got returned-silicon curves they couldn't read, they brought them to you first.

c_startup.title: Your old mentor wants you for a startup
c_startup.situation: Your old mentor has come back from Shanghai with investment to start a small Xiamen company making industrial power chips, and wants you as a partner running design. Sixty percent of your current pay, plenty of options, and the money for the first tape-out is half of what's in the bank.

options.label: Join the startup
options.result: You copied the "Never Again" folder onto the new computer, and on the first day set it as your desktop background.
options.end: From then on you and your mentor made industrial power chips. You saw winters with just one tape-out's worth of money left in the bank, and springs when the first chip ran on a customer's production line. Many years later your chips were inside many machines you never saw, every one of them steady.

options.label: Stay
options.result: You turned it down, but agreed to review the design of their first chip. In his circuit you found a mistake he'd once taught you to avoid, and the two of you laughed over the tea table for a long time.

c_university.title: A university's school of integrated circuits wants you
c_university.situation: A university in Xiamen has founded a school of integrated circuits and wants you as a senior engineer, guiding graduate students through tape-outs and running the school's test platform. Thirty percent less pay, winter and summer holidays, no more racing for silicon; but you'll never again have a chip sold with the company's name on it.

options.label: Go to the university
options.result: To your first class you brought the first LDO you ever drew, still soldered onto that test board. You had them take turns hooking up the oscilloscope to see that flat line.
options.end: You spent many years at the school, taking class after class of students through tape-outs. Every year students graduated into chip companies, and when they came back to visit they'd always say: teacher, my first chip came back too.

options.label: Stay at the company
options.result: You turned it down, but agreed to give two lectures a semester. The first time, you spent an afternoon on package inductance.

c_director.title: Go up for Director of Analog Design / Chief Engineer
c_director.situation: The company wants a Director of Analog Design / Chief Engineer over all its analog design teams, forty or fifty people, answerable for the next product generation's technical roadmap and the risk in every tape-out. You'd negotiate budgets with the boss, process and capacity with the fabs, and roadmaps with major customers; when there's a batch problem, you're the first to step forward.

options.label: Go for it
options.result: At the review you covered three things: which processes to switch, which product lines to stop, and what to hand to AI tools versus what must be drawn by people. The boss asked what you feared most. You said: everyone believing that passing simulation means it's right.

options.label: Don't apply; lead your own team well
options.result: You said you'd rather stay close to the circuits. In their first month the new director came to see you every day, to hear about every chip that had come back over the years.

endings.retire: On your last day you copied your mentor's "Never Again" folder to the youngest person on the team, dozens of your own curves added to it now. You stopped by the test lab. The oscilloscope still showed a load step on a new chip, and the line was flat. You walked out of the park, took the BRT over the bridge, and the light on the sea flickered.
endings.burnout: That year you raced through three tape-outs in a row, and once in the test lab you went faint and a colleague helped you into a chair. You quit and rested at home for most of a year, walking slowly along the Island Ring Road every evening, from Baicheng to Hulishan. The waves broke on the rocks one after another, and you stopped thinking about their frequency.

stages: Under your mentor you own one analog block in a chip: drawing schematics in Virtuoso, running process corners and Monte Carlo in Spectre, working out matching and routing with the layout engineer, doing post-layout simulation. You work most with your mentor and the layout engineer. Whether your circuit goes to layout needs your mentor's signature, and in silicon testing you're the one watching.

You own several blocks in a chip on your own, the LDO, the bandgap, the DC-DC loop: from breaking down the spec into circuits, through layout and design documents, to soldering boards, measuring curves and chasing problems in the test lab once silicon is back. You deal daily with applications and test engineers; at the pre-tape-out review, for the first time, you present yourself.

You own a chip's entire analog section on your own, from spec definition and architecture through silicon testing to mass-production support. You mentor one or two newcomers and review their circuits and layouts; you negotiate specs with customers alongside marketing and applications, and when a customer has a problem, you're the first one called.

You lead seven or eight people and own a product line's circuit architecture and spec definition, deciding who does which chip and which block. You review others' circuits more than you draw your own, and the final signature on whether each chip goes to tape-out is yours. You discuss roadmaps with marketing and customers, and process with the fab.

You run all the company's analog design teams, forty or fifty people, answerable for the next generation's roadmap and the risk in every tape-out. You negotiate budgets with the boss, process and capacity with the fabs, three-year roadmaps with major customers; when there's a batch problem, you stand before the customer. One habit remains: when an important chip comes back, you go to the test lab to look.
work: Your mentor had you run a temperature sweep on the bandgap, from minus forty to a hundred and twenty-five degrees. The curve kicked upward at the hot end, and after an afternoon of digging you found one resistor had the wrong temperature coefficient.
The layout engineer said one capacitor in your circuit was too big to fit. You did the math and switched to Miller compensation: half the area, and five more degrees of phase margin.

A test engineer handed you a test board and said the previous chip's quiescent current was slightly over spec. You traced it along the schematic and found one extra branch of bias current switched on.

The applications engineer said a customer found your LDO too slow to start up. You changed one capacitor in the soft-start circuit and simulated all night. Start-up time went from two milliseconds to three hundred microseconds, with overshoot still in spec.

In silicon testing, the DC-DC's efficiency suddenly dropped five points at one particular input voltage. You swept it point by point in the test lab and found the mode-switching threshold was set too close.

The first time you presented your own block at a pre-tape-out review, you were asked twenty-odd questions and couldn't answer three. You went back and added simulations for all three, and it took a second review before it passed.

A customer wanted an LDO with a quiescent current of just one microamp, and marketing said it could be done. You worked through the night and replied that it could, but the load response would be twice as slow, attaching the simulated curves, and let the customer choose.

The newcomer you mentor used the AI tool to get an op-amp with very high gain and beautiful specs. You had him run five hundred Monte Carlo runs; sixty came back with offset voltage out of spec, and he went back to redefine the constraints.

A chip in mass production had a one-in-a-thousand failure rate at a customer. You brought back dozens of bad units and, with the failure-analysis team, decapped them and looked under the microscope, until you found two metal lines in the layout placed too close.

Two teams both wanted a new process for the next chip. You had each make a test chip of one key block, compared leakage and matching when they came back, chose the more conservative one, and left the other team one more chance to try.

Marketing brought a competitor's datasheet and wanted the same chip in three months. You read it and said you couldn't, but could do one in four months with half the quiescent current. Marketing thought about it overnight and agreed.
You set a rule for the team: any circuit tuned by an AI tool must, before tape-out, have its Bode plot drawn by hand by a person, who signs their name to it.

The fab wanted to raise prices twenty percent and have you lock in next year's capacity in advance. You worked out three options and in the end locked in seventy percent, keeping thirty percent for trying a new fab.

A carmaker came for a supplier audit and asked how you could guarantee no failures for fifteen years. You didn't give a slide deck. You took them to the test lab to see the high-temperature burn-in running, and showed them the "Never Again" folder.

The boss wanted to shut a thin-margin product line that had run five years. You listed its customers one by one, and in the end stopped half of it and gave the other half to a young manager to bring costs down.
past: You went to middle school in Ganzhou, Jiangxi, where your father ran an appliance repair shop in town. You'd often crouch in the shop watching him work along a circuit with a multimeter. He said electricity is like water: wherever it gets blocked, that's where trouble starts.
In the gaokao (college entrance exam) you got into microelectronics at a university in Xi'an. You didn't really know what microelectronics was; it just sounded a bit like your father's shop.

In your second year, analog electronics was your best subject and you came top of the class in the final. The professor said in class: digital circuits are one plus one equals two; analog circuits are one plus one roughly equals two, and the hard part is the "roughly."

You were admitted without exams to a master's in microelectronics at a university in Xiamen, under an advisor in analog circuits. You taped out a chip for the first time on one of his projects. When it came back, the bandgap's temperature drift was three times worse than simulated, and you sat in the lab all night.

In your second year of the master's you interned at this company. The mentor had you not draw anything yet, but go through the schematics of a dozen-plus LDOs he'd drawn over ten years, writing a page on why each was drawn that way.

In autumn recruiting you got offers in Shanghai and Xiamen, the Shanghai one paying twenty percent more. You cycled the Island Ring Road all evening and chose Xiamen, because that mentor said: come, I'll teach you to read test curves.

late.pension_note: Estimate: chip companies in Xiamen mostly pay R&D staff's pension contributions at the upper-middle band of the social-insurance base, well below actual pay, so the basic pension comes to around forty percent of your last monthly salary. The options and the flat from your younger years matter more.
scenes: For the first week of retirement, the first thing you thought on waking was still whether last night's Monte Carlo had finished. After a moment you remembered you'd handed in your server account.
Your old university invited you to talk to graduate students about analog design. You didn't use slides. You brought the "Never Again" folder and went through how each of those chips had failed.

Your grandchild's toy car stopped working. You opened it up, worked along it with a multimeter, and found a rusted contact spring. The child asked how you knew it was there. You said: electricity is like water.
In the first months after quitting, you put the computer away in a cupboard. Every afternoon you went to the market for oysters and came home to learn to make oyster omelets. The first few burned.
You took up jogging along the Island Ring Road, from Baicheng to Zengcuo'an, then sat on the beach afterwards watching the tide come in a little at a time.

An old colleague came over for tea and said most circuits were tuned by AI now, but when silicon came back, someone still had to keep watch in the test lab. You said good, and poured him more Tieguanyin.
In your first year on a different path, every time you charged your phone you wondered whose power chip was inside, and whether its output voltage held steady.

At an industry trade show you saw a new power chip whose datasheet claimed an astonishingly low quiescent current. You held it a long time. The young person at the booth said: our boss designed this; he used to work at your company.

On an errand back in the Torch High-Tech Zone you passed the old company. The satay noodle shop downstairs was still there. The owner recognized you and asked whether you still wanted intestines today.
Back home in Ganzhou, your father's repair shop had long since closed, but the multimeter was still in a drawer. You put in a battery, and its needle still moved.

On an old hard drive you found the test curves from your first tape-out as a student, the temperature drift three times worse than simulated, the curve all crooked. You looked at it a long time, and thought it was rather beautiful.

closing.retire: One evening many years later you sat on your balcony in Haicang as the lights on the island across the water came on one by one, their voltage steady; not one flickered. You made a pot of tea and watched them until it was fully dark.
closing.burnout: Many years later you sat on the rocks beside the Island Ring Road as the tide came in, wave by wave, and went out again, wave by wave. You didn't work out its period. You just watched, until the moon rose out of the sea.
closing.end: Many years later you found the first LDO you ever drew in a drawer, still soldered to that old test board, the solder gone dull. You held it in your palm a while, then put it back.
